summary: Argues that networks do not need to control jitter in order to support isochronous applications such as real-time audio and video. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC argues that a network does not need to control jitter to support applications that use data at regular intervals. A receiver can buffer timestamped data and process it at a steady time if it knows the network's maximum delay and has enough bandwidth.

questions: do isochronous applications require jitter control
how do networks support live audio and video
does an isochronous application need network jitter control
how can a receiver restore regular data timing
why might a network still limit jitter
subtitle: An argument that bounded delay and bandwidth can support isochronous applications.

tldr.problem: The memo addresses the claim that networks must control jitter to support applications that process data at regular intervals.
tldr.mechanism: It argues that a receiver can use timestamps, buffering, and regular application scheduling to restore steady processing when the network provides bandwidth and a known maximum delay.
tldr.outcome: The RFC concludes that network jitter control is not required for this purpose, though it may be useful to reduce buffering in network nodes.

today: RFC 1257 is Informational. It argues that bounded delay and sufficient bandwidth can support isochronous applications without requiring network jitter control.

sections.title: Why Jitter Matters to Regular Data
sections.content:
An isochronous application generates or processes regular amounts of data at fixed intervals. The RFC gives telephones and fixed-rate video codecs as examples. Users may notice changes in the time between data arrivals at the output device; the memo uses “jitter” for this timing variation.

The RFC argues that a network needs sufficient bandwidth and a bound on delay, but does not need to control jitter itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Voice and video applications process data on a regular schedule. The memo asks whether the network must deliver every piece at evenly spaced times.

sections.title: Restoring Regular Timing at the Receiver
sections.content:
The memo's scenario assumes the network can bound the maximum transit delay and the receiver knows that bound. The sender timestamps each piece of data, and the receiver stores pieces in a buffer when they arrive. It processes each piece at the time of its timestamp plus the maximum transit delay.

Under these assumptions, the receiver can process data at regular intervals even when the network's arrival times vary. The memo also discusses regular operating-system scheduling and memory for buffering as requirements of the argument.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver can hold incoming data and use its timestamps to decide when to process each piece. That can produce regular output even if arrival times vary.

sections.title: Implications and Limits
sections.content: The RFC suggests that an internetworking protocol for isochronous applications should likely control delay and bandwidth, not require jitter control. It notes that jitter control may still be useful for other reasons, such as reducing the amount of buffering needed in intermediate network nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo argues that delay and bandwidth limits are enough for the applications it discusses. It also acknowledges that reducing jitter may still help networks use less buffer memory.

sections.title: Status of the Memo
sections.content: RFC 1257 is an informational memo presenting an argument about network support for isochronous applications. It does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC presents an informational argument, not a protocol standard.

references.text: Mills, D., "Measured Performance of the Network Time Protocol in the Internet System", RFC 1128, October 1989.
